Processing"],"is-referenced-by-count":0,"URL":"https://doi.org/10.1109/tip.2026.3683291","type":"journal-article"},{"abstract":"<jats:p>Deep neural networks deployed in digital pathology and medical imaging routinely suffer from catastrophic overconfidence when exposed to data outside their training distribution, including atypical tissue phenotypes, cross-center staining variations, foreign imaging modalities, and acquisition artifacts. Standard classification models optimizing cross-entropy loss provide uncalibrated softmax posteriors that do not reflect predictive unfamiliarity. In this paper, we establish an empirical, reproducible benchmarking framework investigating model reliability across four foundational pillars: (i) confidence calibration via validation-tuned Temperature Scaling, (ii) predictive uncertainty quantification via Deep Ensembles (M=3), (iii) out-of-distribution (OOD) detection across four complementary score formulations (Maximum Softmax Probability, Predictive Entropy, Logit-Based Free Energy, and Penultimate Feature-Space Mahalanobis Distance), and (iv) distribution-free finite-sample guarantees through Split-Conformal Prediction and Selective Risk-Coverage Abstention. Evaluating on standardized biomedical datasets spanning colorectal histology (PathMNIST, N=107,180), microscopic hematology cytology (BloodMNIST, N=17,092), and pediatric chest radiographs (PneumoniaMNIST, N=5,856), we uncover critical structural failure modes in conventional output-space scoring. Specifically, Maximum Softmax Probability and Free Energy collapse on far-OOD radiographic images (AUROC &lt; 17%) due to background feature activation, whereas penultimate feature Mahalanobis distance achieves near-perfect separation (99.99% AUROC on far-OOD radiographs and 96.96% AUROC with 0.04% FPR95 on near-OOD blood cytology). Deep ensembles enhance near-OOD uncertainty estimation (+13.17% AUROC over single networks), and temperature scaling reduces Expected Calibration Error from 7.37% to 6.48% while preserving OOD rank order. Split-conformal prediction provides valid 90.41% empirical coverage with an average prediction set size of 1.54 classes, while selective prediction boosts accuracy from 81.55% to 88.26% by abstaining on the 20% most uncertain inputs.</jats:p>","DOI":"10.2139/ssrn.7598822","type":"posted-content","is-referenced-by-count":0,"title":["Reliable Medical Image Classification Through Out-of-Distribution Detection, Uncertainty Quantification, and Conformal Prediction: A Benchmark on MedMNIST"],"author":[{"ORCID":"https://orcid.org/0009-0004-7111-7326","authenticated-orcid":true,"given":"Paras","family":"Rajput","sequence":"first","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]}],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026]]},"URL":"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7598822"},{"DOI":"10.32614/cran.package.weightederm","title":["weightederm: Weighted Empirical Risk Minimization for Changepoint Regression"],"author":[{"given":"Gabriel","family":"Arpino","sequence":"first","affiliation":[],"role":[{"role":"author","vocabulary":"crossref"}]}],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026,4,22]]},"container-title":["CRAN: Contributed Packages"],"is-referenced-by-count":0,"URL":"https://doi.org/10.32614/cran.package.weightederm","type":"dataset"},{"abstract":"<jats:p>AI systems increasingly shape critical decisions across personal and societal domains. Vision and Image Understanding"],"is-referenced-by-count":0,"URL":"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cviu.2026.104768","type":"journal-article"},{"abstract":"<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Current machine learning methods for medical image analysis primarily focus on developing models tailored for their specific tasks, utilizing data within their target domain. These specialized models tend to be data-hungry and often exhibit limitations in generalizing to out-of-distribution samples. In this work, we show that employing models that incorporate multiple domains instead of specialized ones significantly alleviates the limitations observed in specialized models. We refer to this approach as
                    <jats:italic>multi-domain model</jats:italic>
                    and compare its performance to that of specialized models. For this, we introduce the incorporation of diverse medical image domains, including different imaging modalities like X-ray, MRI, CT, and ultrasound images, as well as various viewpoints such as axial, coronal, and sagittal views. Our findings underscore the superior generalization capabilities of multi-domain models, particularly in scenarios characterized by limited data availability and out-of-distribution, frequently encountered in healthcare applications. The integration of diverse data allows multi-domain models to utilize information across domains, enhancing the overall outcomes substantially. To illustrate, for organ recognition, multi-domain model can enhance accuracy by up to 8% compared to conventional specialized models.
